https://www.globalsecurity.org/wmd/libra.text: Military WMD Menu Introduction Systems Facilities Agencies Operations Countries Hot Documents News Reports Policy Budget Congress Links Intelligence Homeland Security Space Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) Ukraine and Germany discuss joint solutions to support agro-exports amid port blockade Ukraine Government Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine, posted 14 August 2026 09:09 Preserving the harvest, ensuring its export to international markets, and supporting global food security are Ukraine's key tasks under the blockade of seaports. Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine Taras Vysotskyi stated this during an online meeting with Alois Rainer, Federal Minister of Agriculture, Food, and Regional Identity of the Federal Republic of Germany. According to Taras Vysotskyi, in 2026 Ukraine expects to harvest about 80 million tonnes of grain and oilseeds, of which around 60 million tonnes are planned for export. At present, alternative logistics routes allow for the export of about 30 million tonnes. However, these cannot replace maritime routes, and their high cost creates additional financial burdens for Ukrainian producers and exporters. "We are doing everything to restore alternative logistics. But its cost is about EUR 50 per tonne higher, which makes exports unprofitable for Ukrainian farmers. Therefore, we are seeking mechanisms together with importing countries to compensate logistics costs, so that Ukrainian products can continue reaching international markets and countries that need them," Taras Vysotskyi emphasized. He noted that until full maritime exports are restored, proper storage of the new harvest must be ensured. Preliminary estimates show Ukraine needs temporary storage capacity for about 10 million tonnes of agricultural products. Ukraine has already appealed to international partners, including EU member states, for assistance. Taras Vysotskyi thanked Germany for supporting Ukraine's agro-sector and developing alternative export routes. In particular, within the European "Solidarity Lanes" initiative and with German support, new phytosanitary and veterinary laboratories were opened in Izmail. These strengthened the capacity of the Danube cluster to facilitate Ukrainian agro-exports. The parties also discussed Ukraine's European integration. Taras Vysotskyi noted that Ukraine continues working to meet all necessary requirements and be ready to join the European Union, expecting the opening of Negotiation Cluster 5, which covers agricultural policy and food. Mr Alois Rainer expressed support for Ukraine and its agricultural sector. He stated that Germany wiould consider ways to assist with Ukrainian agro-exports under the blockade of traditional maritime routes caused by systematic russian attacks on port infrastructure. As a result of the meeting, the parties agreed to continue dialogue on trade, logistics, exports, and European integration of Ukraine's agro-sector. Vysotskyi and Rainer plan to hold a bilateral meeting during the EU Council on Agriculture and Fisheries (AGRIFISH) in September 2026.

http://www.bgnes.com/science/nasa-s-new-.text: Now that NASA’s “Nancy Grace Roman” space telescope has set course for its final destination, more and more of the mission’s scientific goals are beginning to take shape. Among them is the possibility that the telescope could discover an Earth-like planet orbiting a star similar to our Sun using the method of gravitational microlensing, according to the website “The Debrief.” The mission team believes that such a discovery could help identify targets for the future “Habitable Worlds” observatory. It could study the atmospheres of such planets in search of biosignatures—chemical traces that could indicate the presence of life. Among the key questions facing the Roman mission are how common planetary systems similar to our own are, what kinds of planets exist in the cold outer regions of these systems, and what determines the habitability of Earth-like worlds. Scientists use several methods to detect exoplanets, but “Roman” will rely on three main approaches—the transit method, gravitational microlensing, and direct imaging. NASA expects that combining these methods will lead to the discovery of about 100,000 new exoplanets—a huge leap from the nearly 6,200 planets known today. “We hope that ‘ROMAN’ will discover thousands of new exoplanets and significantly expand our knowledge of the diversity of planetary systems in our Galaxy,” said Assoc. Prof. Edita Stonkutė, an astrophysicist at Vilnius University who is not part of the mission team. Gravitational microlensing can detect Earth-like planets around Sun-like starsMost known exoplanets have been discovered using the transit method—scientists detect a slight dip in a star’s brightness when the planet passes in front of it as seen from Earth. “ROMAN” will use this approach for most of its discoveries. Gravitational microlensing, however, also allows for the detection of planets that are difficult to observe by other means. The phenomenon occurs when two distant stars align almost in a straight line relative to the observer. The gravity of the closer star bends the light from the more distant star, briefly amplifying it. “If the alignment is particularly precise, the closer star acts as a cosmic lens that focuses and magnifies the light from the background star. By analyzing these changes, astronomers can detect the presence of a planet and estimate its mass and orbital characteristics,” explained Stonkute. Microlensing is not limited to systems involving stars. Similar events can also be caused by exoplanets. Using its wide-angle camera, “Roman” will observe hundreds of millions of stars. The telescope will search for extremely small and short-lived increases in starlight that may indicate the occurrence of a microlensing event. The transit method is particularly well-suited for detecting larger exoplanets, while microlensing can detect planets similar to those in the Solar System, including worlds with masses comparable to that of Mars, located in the habitable zone of their star or even farther out. The habitable zone is the region around a star where conditions could allow liquid water to exist on a planet’s surface—a key factor for life as we know it. “Microlensing is particularly valuable because it can detect planets that are difficult to observe using other methods. This includes small, Earth-like planets located far from their star,” said Stonkute. The ROMAN team hopes to discover more than 1,000 planets using this method. Microlensing events generally cannot be predicted in advance. That is precisely why telescopes must constantly observe vast swaths of the sky to increase the likelihood of detecting such an event. “This is where Roman has an advantage over other telescopes that have searched for exoplanets using different methods,” the astrophysicist emphasized. Although “ROMAN” will be capable of directly imaging some exoplanets, the discovery of a second Earth orbiting a Sun-like star will likely occur indirectly—primarily through a gravitational microlensing event. NASA describes the mission as an important step toward the concept of the future “Habitable Worlds” space observatory. The project is still awaiting final approval, but its goal is to enable the first-ever direct imaging of Earth-like planets. “Roman” could also contribute to the study of the atmospheres of exoplanets discovered using the transit method. The telescope will search for potential biosignatures by analyzing atmospheric gases, including oxygen and ozone, whose presence could be linked to biological processes. Thus, the “Nancy Grace Roman” mission will not merely expand the catalog of known exoplanets. It may help scientists determine which of them are the most promising candidates for future searches for conditions suitable for life—including a potential “second Earth.” | BGNES

https://newsroomamerica.com/a/Gb5irHvCOj.text: Library of Congress Music Division Holds a Handful of Casts From Famous Pianists and Composers 30 Oct 2026 9:16 a.m. · Source: U.S. Library of Congress The Library of Congress Music Division holds roughly a half dozen casts of the hands of famous pianists and composers, most of them plaster, according to a press release from the Library. The collection includes a cast of violinist and composer Charles Martin Loeffler's hand gripping the neck of a torso-less violin. Loeffler's "Canticle of the Sun" was the second piece heard in the Coolidge Auditorium on October 28, 1925, immediately following J.S. Bach's "To God on high all glory be," BWV 715. A pair of plaster casts preserves the hands of Erich Wolfgang Korngold, whose musical output is held largely in the Library's Erich Wolfgang Korngold Collection. That collection includes correspondence, business papers, programs and photographs in addition to many of his extant manuscripts. The right hand of Ignace Jan Paderewski, the famed Polish pianist and politician, is also held. Researchers can explore photographs, programs and writings in the Helena Liibke Collection on Ignace Paderewski, with further materials including programs, caricatures and correspondence sprinkled throughout its holdings. The Library also holds the bronzed hands of Danny Kaye, realia from the Danny Kaye and Sylvia Fine Collection. Despite not reading music, Kaye drew on his innate musicality to conduct orchestras to help them raise money, with Victor Borge-like antics added to his routine. Rafael Joseffy, best known as a pianist but also an influential pedagogue, composer and editor, is represented by a plaster cast of his right hand created by Anna Marie Dorthea in 1915, held in its own nest-like bed. The Library also holds drafts and sketches of his technical exercises related to his "School of Advanced Piano Playing." The final cast in the survey belongs to Nicolai Medtner. The Library holds several of his manuscripts, including his piano quintet, which he worked on for over forty years and which was acquired not long ago. The Coolidge Auditorium will host the first performance of the piece, with the manuscript on display, on Friday, November 13 at 8 p.m., featuring the Bennewitz Quartet with pianist Arsentiy Kharitonov. The Library said visitors can come to the Performing Arts Reading Room for a more hands-on encounter with its collection items. ← Back to latest
